memory_candidates.content: When triaging a corpus-wide SC2034 ('appears unused') shellcheck sweep: before deciding disable-vs-delete for any flagged name, run `grep -rn '<name>' <scan-root>` to check for external sourcers/callers first. Disable with a one-line reason (never delete) when the name is: (a) an exported constant/array consumed by other files that `source` this one (confirm via the grep); (b) a closed-over global a sourced FUNCTION reads, even though the assignment site itself never uses `$name` textually -- shellcheck's SC2034 is per-file name-reference analysis, so a fixture that pre-seeds a global before calling a function defined in a DIFFERENT sourced file will still be flagged, even though the function genuinely reads it; (c) a documented calling-convention positional parameter (e.g. every extension's own context-injection hook receives the same 5 args from one dispatcher, even if a specific hook body doesn't need all of them); (d) a bounded-iteration-counter loop variable (`for i in 1 2 3; do ... done` where only the repeat count matters, never `$i`'s value); (e) a variable assignment required ONLY to get the `if VAR=$(cmd); then` idiom's set-e-safe exit-code capture, where the captured text itself is discarded. Delete only when exhaustively confirmed dead: zero `$name`/`${name...}` references anywhere in the file, and no external consumer found by the grep.

A `# shellcheck disable=SCxxxx` directive only suppresses the finding on the SINGLE PHYSICAL LINE immediately following it, UNLESS that next line opens a compound command (if/while/for/case/a function definition), in which case the suppression extends to every line inside that compound. Two concrete traps discovered repeatedly while wiring disables into an existing corpus: (1) placing the directive before an `elif` branch, a `case` arm's own opening line, or a `done`/`fi`/`esac` terminator is a hard shellcheck PARSE ERROR (SC1073/SC1123/SC1124/SC1085) -- the directive must go before the compound command's OPENING line (the `if`, the `case` statement's own `in` line, the `while`) to cover a site nested inside one of its branches; (2) placing the directive before one statement in a sequence of several (e.g. `VAR1=...` then `VAR2=...` then `VAR3=...`, each separately flagged) only covers VAR1 -- VAR2 and VAR3 each need their OWN preceding directive line, even when they are visually adjacent and conceptually one unit.

A task's creation-time file_scope (from state.json, enumerated by research/planning from named heaviest files) can under-enumerate a task whose full file list is only discoverable by actually RUNNING a tool against the live tree mid-implement (e.g. a corpus-wide lint sweep finding every file with any violation, not just the ones named in the research report's heaviest-files list). git-commit-phase.sh's Containment Self-Check silently drops any touched path not in the declared file_scope from the commit (with a WARNING easy to read past), so the file can remain genuinely uncommitted after a commit call reports success. update-task-status.sh's --file-scope-add flag implements the sanctioned 'Unknown-Footprint Convention' merge (`.file_scope = ((.file_scope // []) + $add | unique)`), but is RESTRICTED to operation==postflight && target_status in {research,plan} and cannot be invoked mid-implement. The workaround: call state-write.sh directly with the IDENTICAL jq filter the restricted flag uses internally, scoped to the task's own project_number, then re-run the phase commit -- it picks up the previously-dropped files cleanly. Always verify with `git status --short -- <touched-paths>` after a phase commit claims success, especially on a task whose scope was only fully discoverable at implementation time.
